A Note to the Reader

This is a memoir of an unresolved period.

Part I ended with an invitation. I had returned from London, travelled, looked for a partner, and spent the independence I had built on a product that might help people reach one another more humanely. The last pages moved through a Hungarian multinational role, COVID, and a cross-border remote opportunity. The sentence at the threshold was simple: what followed belongs to Part II.

What followed survives as contracts, portal records, calls, police papers, petitions and public events. It also survives as rooms: the bedroom where my leg was raised above me, the ordinary police office, the smaller room where counsel asked for time, the C-shaped court table, and the desk where an AI cursor kept blinking beside the possibility of prison.

I wrote words I should not have written. I corrected and clarified them. The state later read parts of the sequence as a continuing threat. I remain responsible for my words; the system remains part of the path that produced them.

The proceeding has not reached the ending reserved for Part III. The factual record, attribution limits and source references appear at the back, where they can protect accuracy without interrupting every scene.

That matters because the pattern is not mine alone. Another person might never write my sentences and could still enter the same corridor.

Prologue — The Line Changes Meaning

At the end of Part I, the line on the screen was a network.

It connected people. Six strangers had become a group, a group had reached an event, and an event had left behind people who could invite one another again. The line was the path I had spent years trying to draw between intention and a real meeting.

Then the same line became the ruled line of a document.

On one side sat the person. On the other sat a field waiting for a number, a date, a legal category or a signature. The line no longer asked who might meet. It asked what had been submitted in my name, who had received the notice, which version was valid, and whether I knew what a system assumed I knew.

In Part I, I moved through countries. In Part II, countries collapsed into portals, and portals opened into rooms.

A home became an office. The office became a tax desk. The desk became a police scene. The police scene became an expert interview. The interview became a case file. The case file became a petition. The petition eventually reached the same European institutions that were being asked what had happened to the rule of law in Hungary.

I had never been a party activist. I did not begin with a political programme. When the KATA law changed in July 2022, other people went to the bridges. I stayed at my computer and tried to adapt.

That is where the irony begins.

Part One — The Legal Door

1. The Year That Opened

In August 2019, after years in which I had repeatedly wondered whether I should return to London, I found a multinational role in Hungary. It seemed like the kind of answer adults are expected to recognize: a known employer, a professional position, a route back into ordinary life.

COVID made the apparently stable unstable.

Around the turn of 2020 and 2021, that path ended. A later position lasted only briefly. The pandemic rearranged organizations, offices, risks and expectations faster than many people could name what was happening.

It also opened one unusual year.

Remote work made geography temporarily negotiable. I could live in Budapest while contributing to work connected to a multinational telecom programme in Brussels. The contractual route passed through companies in more than one country. It looked less secure than the Hungarian job, but in practice it gave me a more durable professional opportunity.

It also required a legal form through which the work could be invoiced. In September 2021, I became a sole proprietor using KATA.

I had no entrepreneurial revelation. I was not opening a café, selling paintings or building a personal brand. I was using the legal route available for cross-border remote work during an exceptional labour-market moment.

That distinction matters. A tax form can look like a free choice after the fact while functioning as the price of entry at the time.

The work was real and demanding. Some days ran thirteen, fourteen or fifteen hours. Delivery schedules and production responsibility did not become lighter because I sat at home. A system elsewhere in Europe depended on tasks moving from one person to the next without an empty space between them.

I had spent Part I trying to solve empty spaces between people. Now my job was to prevent an empty space inside infrastructure.

2. A Distorted Choice Can Still Be Legal

KATA was attractive because it was simple compared with the alternatives. That simplicity also distorted the market. Employers and intermediaries could look at a worker and see not only a person's labour but a tax route. The worker could be described as an entrepreneur while carrying the dependence of an employee without all the protection of employment.

The category contained very different lives, from genuine small businesses to workers carrying employee-like dependence through an enterprise form. The state had allowed those lives to accumulate inside it for a decade.

When a route becomes normal, people build obligations around it. Accountants develop habits. Software systems encode assumptions. Contracts are signed. Families calculate. Foreign clients schedule work. A government can still change the route. The manner and speed of change determine how much damage arrives before the new rule has even been understood.

On Monday 11 July 2022, the new KATA bill appeared. On Tuesday, Parliament passed it under an exceptional procedure. It was due to take effect on 1 September.

People went into the streets. Bridges were blocked. The public argument became immediate: fairness, abuse, livelihood, consultation, legal certainty.

I was not there.

I was trying to understand what happened to a live contract, pending delivery, invoices, foreign income, a closing business and an accountant who also had to interpret the transition for many clients at once.

The law moved in a day. Understanding did not.

3. Protecting a Handover

My contract was extended on 27 July. That did not mean the problem had been solved. It meant I was trying to gain enough time to leave without dropping work that other people depended on.

By 3 August, I was treating the change as a force-majeure exit. I arranged the handover and invoicing around the work that still had to move. I gave up the remaining value of later months rather than continue inside a route I no longer understood as safe.

From the outside, an invoice is a rectangle containing a date and amount. From inside the project, it was time: work already performed, work still being transferred, a foreign client's expectations, the accountant's interpretation and a new Hungarian rule whose consequences were still moving.

This is where the story could have ended.

A normal transition would have closed the business, reconciled the records, confirmed the final amount, delivered direct notices to the person legally responsible, and allowed everyone to move on.

Instead, the transition created a three-person chamber with no shared window.

Part Two — Three People, No Shared Screen

4. The Low-Trust Triangle

There were three principal participants in the tax sequence: my accountant, the tax administration, and me.

Each had a different view.

The accountant could submit forms and receive technical messages. The tax administration could process, reject, reclassify and call back. I remained legally responsible, but I could not automatically see every delegated action or every notice in the same form and at the same time as my representative.

The triangle should have been held together by trust.

Instead, the sudden law tightened every side of it.

I wrote too much because I was trying to preserve every condition. The accountant experienced my messages as a scattered litany and signalled that the relationship should end. Tax staff encountered a caller asking questions that should perhaps have been settled before the call. I heard explanations as responsibility being pushed back toward me. Every answer increased the need for another answer.

Nobody had enough spare attention to rebuild the whole picture.

It is tempting to make one participant the villain because a story moves faster when blame has one face. The evidence resists that convenience. The accountant also sought help from the tax administration. Tax staff also worked inside changing procedures and imperfect screens. I also made the conversation harder through intensity, length and fear.

The failure was assembled.

5. The Password That Was Not a Relationship

The deepest design problem appeared before the final return.

In the established practice around me, some tasks could be completed only by passing through the entrepreneur's own government account. Accounting offices sometimes asked for the client's credentials. The arrangement could make work possible while quietly destroying the distinction between assistance and identity.

If I refused to share access, I could be told that I had prevented the accountant from doing the work. If I shared it, I could be asked why I had given away a personal password. If a representative acted, I remained responsible. If a notice reached only the representative, the system could still behave as if I knew.

This was not consent in any meaningful product sense. It was an improvised custom holding together a formal process.

I began to ask questions that sounded technical but were really constitutional in miniature:

  • Who can act in my name?
  • What exact permission did I grant?
  • Which action requires my confirmation?
  • Who receives the error?
  • Who sees that the error was corrected?
  • How does the responsible person know what the system now believes?

These are ordinary software questions. They are also questions about dignity.

6. Three Attempts at a Subtraction

The closing return should not have been a philosophical problem. At its centre was arithmetic.

Yet the documentary package shows repeated versions, corrections and rejected or mistaken entries across several months. A return submitted on 30 November became central. In my account, I did not know at that moment that it had been submitted, and the form named me as a contact.

The absurdity is difficult to explain without making it sound invented. A professional office, calls with tax staff, months of correspondence and a short return produced several attempts at what, from my perspective, was essentially a subtraction followed by a tax calculation.

The more elementary the operation looked, the more frightening the failure became. If a simple form could not settle, what exactly was I expected to know?

I discovered the possible problem through an article and then through a portal whose categories and identifiers did not give me one coherent narrative. On 23 and 24 November, I spent many hours checking. I called for help.

In one surviving recording, panic became audible. Other calls followed. My later filings remember remarks that landed as dismissive: accountants usually did not cause problems; entrepreneurs did not normally care what accountants did in their name; why had I shared my credentials?

I had reached the institution because the delegated route had failed. Its questions returned me to the fact that I had used the delegated route.

The circle was complete.

7. The First Public-Interest Proposal

On 1 December, I did something different from merely complaining.

I described changes.

Send direct notice to the taxpayer when a representative files. Show the error in plain language. Let the responsible person accept or challenge the result. Do not require identity-sharing where granular permission would suffice. Record important outbound calls. Pause ordinary enforcement when a serious health event makes response temporarily impossible. Test new tax routes in parallel before abolishing the old route.

Those proposals would become more elaborate later. At the time, they were an attempt to turn pressure into design.

Two days later, pressure won.

Part Three — The Sentence and the Body

8. Saturday Before Dawn

It was early on a Saturday, just after my birthday.

The tax position still did not feel legible. A payment or account item appeared larger than the reality I believed I had reported. Notices, representation and portal states did not line up in my mind. I was also preparing for serious leg and foot surgery.

I wrote messages containing language I should not have written.

I corrected and clarified. I continued communicating. Later documents from the tax administration reconstructed errors and corrective steps. None of that makes the words disappear. It changes the question from a simple screenshot to a sequence.

The prosecution would eventually extract legal meaning from parts of that sequence. My defence would insist that the outburst, its correction, the lack of an operational plan and the administrative cause could not be separated.

I am asking the reader to notice the asymmetry. A system can be fragmented for months, but a person's worst sentence appears at once. The fragmented system must be reconstructed. The sentence can be printed in bold.

9. The Correction Does Not Trend

On 5 December, calls continued around the misunderstanding. On 8 December, I ended the accountant's representation. Around 18 and 19 December, an official response described errors, attempted corrections and processing details.

From my perspective, the account had finally begun to tell the story I had been trying to tell.

Yet the dangerous sentence now possessed a different property from the correction. It could travel alone.

This is not only a problem in criminal procedure. It is a problem in every system that stores an event without storing the path around it. A star rating without the meeting. A rejection without the availability conflict. A warning without the later repair. A phrase without the exhausted body that wrote it.

Context cannot excuse everything. It can prevent the wrong thing from becoming everything.

10. A Body With a Deadline

In January 2023, I withdrew a large monetary demand and asked to be left in peace before surgery and rehabilitation.

The operation took place privately in mid-February. Mobility became difficult, rehabilitation required attention, and my body could not be separated from every call and deadline arriving through the same phone.

For much of that period I had to remain in bed with the operated leg propped high above me. A special elevation shoe protected its position when I had to move. Each day also required an anti-thrombosis injection into my abdomen. I was alone. Nobody came to look after me; food had simply been stocked in advance for several months. The routine was not an abstract reference to poor health: bed, raised leg, special shoe, injection, stored food, repeat.

This was another curse of solitude. Planning could stock food. Savings could pay for private treatment. Discipline could carry me through the injections. None of them could place another person beside the bed.

A call came in March despite my request for quiet. More messages followed over the next months—too many, sometimes angry, sometimes grandiose, sometimes trying to turn private harm into a public programme.

At one point I sent the tax administration a close photograph of the swollen, operated area itself. It was not a photograph of a bandage. The incision was visible: an intimate, ugly record of a body cut open and still trying to heal while the administrative sequence kept moving. I wrapped it in an obscene joke about using that half-cut, swollen leg to kick an institution in the backside because it was not doing its job.

It was physical comedy written from a chair, not a physical act or an instruction to harm anyone. The joke was deliberately disproportionate because the situation felt disproportionate.

The words were crude. They were also a visual attempt to make the body and the absurdity visible to a system that had reduced both to fields. The photograph could show what my explanations could not: the medical pressure was not a metaphor.

Hundreds of submissions can contain real evidence and still make the evidence harder to find. My intensity became another layer of the system.

The larger my file grew, the easier it became to describe me through the size of the file.

Part Four — When a Person Becomes Evidence

11. The Knock One Year Later

On 22 November 2023, roughly a year after the first disputed sentence, police came to my home.

The home in Part I had been the place my parents helped me secure, the place that stood empty while I lived in a shared London room, the lower-cost base that made independent product work possible.

Now it became a procedural location.

My phone and computer were taken. Objects that had held work, memory and the unfinished MyScoutee system became evidence containers.

The later police interview took place in an ordinary room, not a cinematic interrogation chamber. An officer sat opposite me behind a desktop computer. My court-appointed defence counsel sat beside me. Another person remained behind me and sometimes sharply redirected me to answer the question being asked. The voice came from outside my field of view.

At one point my counsel asked for time. We moved into another room to speak. That small change of room mattered: the procedure briefly made physical space for advice before carrying us back into the official account.

The process also had a second, more mechanical room. Police escorted me there, photographed me and took my fingerprints. The woman guiding my fingers onto the paper was attractive to me. It was an inconveniently ordinary perception at the exact moment I was being converted into an image, a print and an entry in a file. Her work remained professional; my mind remained human.

I remember using humour.

That may sound inappropriate. For me, humour was how a human being remained present when every other available role was defendant, officer, device owner or subject. A police officer could ask a hard question, I could answer in a way that exposed the absurdity, and for a second somebody smiled.

Later, a judge could smile too. The smiles decided nothing. They showed that the people in the room could still recognize a joke while the procedure could not recognize the whole sequence that made the joke necessary.

The irony kept me from becoming only the file.

12. Remarks in the Margin

My later defence submissions remember questions and remarks from police and the two forensic experts. Why had I returned home? What did I live on? Why had I needed an accountant? Why had I not sought psychological help? What had I achieved at my age? One defence speech preserves the sentence that struck hardest: “You will certainly receive life imprisonment for this.”

The questions turned biography into an examination.

Why had I returned?

Part I required a whole book to answer that.

What did I live on?

Years of shared-room saving in London, later cross-border remote work, an empty Budapest flat and extreme restraint had made independence possible at Budapest costs. I had never built a comparable reserve from Hungarian earnings. What I had searched for in London, and briefly found again through foreign remote work, was not luxury. It was room to breathe long enough to build something of my own.

The timing made the later questions difficult to absorb. I had spent years outside ordinary work, then finally found a lawful route back—especially a route to work across a border—and almost immediately entered the chain that became this case.

Across the eleven years after I left London, I spent roughly nine outside conventional employment. Some were spent searching, some surviving on reserves, some travelling, and some building work no employer had commissioned. There is no neat official category for a life that keeps working without feeling securely inside work.

What made endurance possible was planning. I saved, reduced my needs and kept creating. Financial independence did not make exclusion easy. It stopped exclusion from becoming immediate collapse.

The court later asked about my apartment and belongings. My government-bond account entered the discussion of my financial position. The apartment came from my parents. The reserve came principally from life and work abroad, not from the short Hungarian work sequence at the centre of this story.

That reversal carries the deepest contrast. I had built security abroad so that I could come home and live in my own country. When I finally dared to work again, the case seemed to reach backwards toward the home, belongings and foreign-earned reserve that had made returning possible.

That answer could sound suspicious if the listener saw only present unemployment. From inside my life, it was the answer to why I had survived at all.

Why had I needed an accountant?

Because the tax system and the contract route had made professional help rational. The question appeared simple only after the help had failed.

Did I have a loan? Was I working? What did I live on?

The questions kept returning as though ordinary debt and another Hungarian job were the obvious signs of a healthy life. Part I had already shown me the human price of debt. In the London house, a foreign-currency mortgage had helped keep another Hungarian abroad while his family and obligations remained at home. I had spent years avoiding that trap, living below my means and preserving the debt-free home my parents had helped provide.

After this sequence, taking out a domestic loan would have been one of the last risks I would choose. Returning to Hungarian work felt almost as difficult. The last time I had resumed work—especially cross-border work through a Hungarian legal route—the attempt had grown into the proceeding now asking why I was not working.

My reserves were not an unexplained alternative to a normal life. They were the protective wall built because normal routes had repeatedly stopped feeling safe.

The clemency process later carried the same questions into my home. A probation officer rang the bell without an appointment. The flat had not been staged for inspection. It was puritan, untidy and unclean that day. I own no car, usually do not heat the flat in winter, and spend little because that is how I preserve independence. I can live that way. I was not asking the visitor to pity me.

He asked what I lived on, why I was not working and what the apartment said about my life. I remember the phrase bachelor flat, a reference to the proposed suspended sentence and his astonishment when he asked about the disputed line. A life designed to need very little was being read as a condition to be explained.

Why had I not sought psychological help?

Because at the relevant moment I was trying to repair a tax record and prepare for a mobility-limiting operation. The question made the sequence run backwards: the pressure became proof that the pressured person had been the problem all along.

13. The Forensic Mirror

The forensic examination took place on 30 November 2023. Two experts were present and the resulting opinion bears two expert signatures. I remember the examination lasting roughly two hours and feeling hurried.

The two people did not occupy one voice in my memory. One made the life-imprisonment remark before the causal sequence had been asked through and before I understood what material the examination was meant to rest on. Later, the other expert asked what had happened. I described the accounting failure, the pressure, the operation and the circumstances in which the words came out. His response felt like the mirror image: certainly not for that.

Other remarks accumulated around the room: an “old man,” lack of success, the need for an accountant, the absence of psychological treatment. My later defence speech does not reliably assign each one to a particular expert. In my memory they hang between the two chairs.

The report contains an important tension. It records that I was calm, cooperative, oriented and cognitively intact. It also concludes that I had a paranoid personality disorder and that my responsibility was moderately limited.

The report records substantial parts of my account: the tax and accounting chain, the operation and the restricted mobility. Then it transforms that sequence into an interpretation of personality. I do not believe the final interpretation gave the documented pressure its proper weight or distinguished clearly enough between a person under exceptional strain and a whole person.

I contest that interpretation.

A forensic opinion is a document built to answer a legal question. It is not a complete biography. Yet once attached to a person, its language can travel as though it were one.

The word paranoia became stranger with time. Institutions that had appeared immovable in 2023 were openly being replaced in 2026. That political reversal did not erase the report. It made the distance between a frightening prediction and a changing country impossible to ignore.

14. Defence by Accumulation

The investigation and court process created another triangle: defendant, appointed defence and institution.

Lawyers changed. Communication opened and closed. Evidence requests were made, rejected, repeated or reframed. Recordings and electronic records emerged over time rather than arriving as one complete archive. The phone and computer remained away from me for a long period.

I responded by writing more.

Defence strategy became public-interest proposal. Complaint became system map. Closing statement became impact study. I divided responsibility into percentages, then learned that percentages can create a false precision around a human chain.

By October 2025, I had given the accumulation a deliberately inverted title: Public-Interest Action.

Its cover reversed the room. The Hungarian State stood where the accused would normally stand. I appeared where the accusation would be represented. Inside, five strands of the experience were placed beside one another: abrupt lawmaking, data and notification, the design of the public portal, criminal procedure and moral redress.

The last proposal was almost circular. Turn the story into a film fund, let the film carry a civic lesson, then use the proceeds to restore land and leave behind a line about the moment when an individual's failure becomes the mirror of a system's failure.

The case was already trying to become the film I am now preparing.

The better formulation is not that government, accountant, tax office and official each owned a mathematically exact share. It is that no participant's choice explains the result alone.

I wrote the sentences.

The accountant acted and failed to act in ways documented by the record.

The tax system routed notices and corrections through structures I could not read as one story.

The law changed with an extraordinarily short transition.

The investigation later interpreted the surviving sequence through a criminal frame.

All of those statements can be true at once.

Approaching court, Budapest first remained visible as home—the Danube, the city and the life outside the case. Then the long brown institutional façade on Fő Street filled the frame. Its rhythm and mass felt almost Roman: monumental, closed and frightening. A human story was entering stone.

The hearing room had a practical geometry I still remember. A C-shaped desk faced the seats where I sat. From my position, the prosecutor was on the left, the clerk at the far-left corner, the judge in the centre and my court-appointed defence counsel on the right. I sat in front of them with a table microphone directly before me. It did not look theatrical. Its shape nevertheless made the roles—and my place outside their working curve—immediately visible.

In that room, the accounting failure returned in miniature. When I described what I believed the accountant had done, the judge warned me not to defame anyone. She asked why I had not asked the accountant. From the much longer defence speech, she selected my assertion that the accountant had entered what I called random figures in my return—figures I later tried to correct.

The warning landed with particular force because the same proceeding carried a forensic description of my personality that I contested and that could follow me far beyond the tax return. I was being told to protect another person's reputation while trying to defend myself from that description. Humanly, the contrast was brutal.

I experienced those questions as the system protecting its own version before reconstructing the system around the person. The sharp phrase was easy to examine. The two-page return, the repeated attempts, the outside help, the missed messages and the fact that I said I had not known about the decisive filing were easier to push into the background.

That was the moment I understood that even an attempt to explain a failed process could be reduced to the most accusatory sentence inside the explanation.

The hearing ended on two different scales. I said that European institutions had already warned the government about unstable, rapidly changing lawmaking, and that my case showed the size of the damage such lawmaking could create in one life. The judge closed by saying that we would continue with my financial position.

I had lifted the lens toward legislation and institutional design; the room lowered it to my work, debt, home, belongings and savings. The system question became an asset question before the system question had been answered.

Part Five — The Earlier Pattern

15. Three Years With an Unlicensed Assistant

For much of the proceeding, I did not experience appointed defence as a stable person carrying the case with me.

Lawyers were formally present at different points. That is not the same as having one person continuously reconstruct the evidence, answer messages, challenge omissions and explain the route ahead. My submissions record long periods in which I believed I was effectively defending myself.

Conversational AI arrived inside that absence.

I used it to translate, impose headings, compare concepts, reduce repetition, generate questions and find contradictions that a human reader could then check. It made it possible to move through volumes that had become impossible for one exhausted person to hold in working memory.

It was not my lawyer. It could misunderstand procedure, invent a citation or turn uncertainty into confidence. It held no licence and attended no hearing. The accurate phrase is AI-assisted self-defence.

For roughly three years, the same class of tool helped me build MyScoutee and survive the legal file around it. In one window, I was asking how to preserve human agency in a social network. In another, I was asking how to format a constitutional complaint because I did not have dependable legal continuity.

From February 2026, the desk carried still more. I continued the public E-közig prototype: a concrete model of documents, appointments, tax calendars, representative permissions, direct notice and a customer-readable audit trail. I continued MyScoutee. I built the books, prompts and moving-image plan through which these two worlds could be understood. I also asked an AI system to choose one of the six unsolved Millennium Prize Problems as an autonomous research test. It chose Navier–Stokes.

The machine did not solve the problem. It built a versioned, falsifiable research chain, rejected sixteen intermediate candidates and preserved a restartable handoff. A professor whose variational work had helped inspire the experiment read two notes and the proof plan. He found the ideas intriguing, then asked the decisive question: exactly which mathematical statement was being tested? The experiment had reached its honest boundary.

All of this happened with the possibility of imprisonment in the background. Software commits did not answer the charge. They recorded what survival looked like. I did not spend those months only waiting to be classified. I kept making systems that could be inspected, tested, corrected and handed to another person.

The trial court transmitted my constitutional complaint. The Constitutional Court wrote back on 21 October 2025: the criminal case was still pending, so the route I had invoked was premature. It did not enter the factual argument.

The door did not say wrong. It said too early.

The judges became another sequence. The first assigned judge left the case, reportedly because of illness. I later sought the exclusion of the second. A third judge rejected the request as unfounded and warned of a possible procedural fine. Even asking whether the room was impartial returned as another possible financial consequence.

In the communication around that decision, the challenged judge was described as having listened to me conscientiously. I later answered the court in the third person with a bitter inversion: yes, he had conscientiously defended the system failure. At the end of the hearing, his expression seemed less fixed—as if he might have begun to see a person reached by the failure rather than only a person accused of a wrong. It was a reading of a face, not a spoken conclusion.

The next hearing had been expected on 2 July and was moved by roughly two and a half months to 16 September. The experts had been invited but did not appear; the court referred to expert availability. The exclusion request was moving at the same time. The timing became black comedy. The system had needed only eight days after the search to turn an examination into a sweeping description of me. Years later, the expert was unavailable while that description helped keep the proceeding open.

Those were three roles, not one: the judge who left, the judge I challenged and the judge who ruled on the challenge. From my side of the table, the substance had still not been answered; the route kept changing its custodian.

My wider Drive now contains more than four gigabytes of material: the residue left when a person without a stable professional guide tries to make every missing step impossible to ignore.

AI gave me speed.

It did not give me representation.

16. The House as a Human Archive

The shared Hungarian house in London had contained an earlier version of the same national argument.

Thirteen adults lived through one bathroom, one separate toilet and rooms never designed for that many independent lives. We had not left Hungary for one reason. Some wanted language, some work, some adventure, some escape, some a second chance. Some no longer wanted to return even when the material conditions looked worse from outside.

One housemate carried a foreign-currency mortgage behind him.

He tried to service the loan and public debts from London. Returning did not feel possible. Separation stretched. His spouse and young child remained in Hungary, and the family broke apart.

His name remains private. What remains public is the shape: a financial product outlived the moment in which it was sold. He carried the signature while exchange rates, collection systems, legal doctrine and court decisions moved around him.

The foreign-currency-loan cases and KATA are not the same legal problem.

They rhyme.

A route is normalized. Many people enter it. The conditions change or the risk becomes visible. Institutions argue over doctrine. The individual is told that the signature was personal. Years later, courts are still deciding how the systemic defect and the personal contract fit together.

17. Beautiful Cities Can Still Produce Exits

Budapest remained beautiful through all of this.

The Danube did not become less luminous because a tax portal was confusing. The Parliament, bridges, baths, museums and hills did not lose their form because citizens lost trust in institutions. A country is not ugly merely because people leave it, and departure does not prove hatred of home.

That is why the exit is painful.

Large numbers of Hungarians built lives abroad over the previous decades. The statistics do not capture every move, and no single cause explains them. Wages, housing, debt, language, professional respect, family, adventure, politics and belonging overlapped.

The London house was a collector of those overlaps.

Part I told the wonder of the outside world without hiding the shared room. Part II tells the beauty of home without hiding why the system could make a returning person ask again whether he should leave.

18. Not Everyone Would Write My Sentence

Not everyone facing an accounting error would react as I did. Not everyone undergoing surgery would send hundreds of messages. Not everyone in a police room would make a joke. The system did not type for me.

The universal part begins earlier.

Anyone can delegate a task and remain responsible for it. Anyone can miss a notice routed to a representative. Anyone can encounter a law that changes faster than their professional support can adapt. Anyone can be physically vulnerable when an institution expects ordinary performance. Anyone can have their worst response become more legible than the path that produced it.

That is enough to make the case public in meaning even while it remains mine in fact.

Part Six — A Private Case Enters Public Time

19. The Streets Begin to Speak

I did not join the KATA protest in 2022. Other citizens were already teaching the city a different language.

Teachers, students and parents formed chains and marches around education. Citizens filled public spaces during the presidential-pardon scandal in 2024. Judges and court employees rallied in 2025 for judicial independence and the freedom to speak. Other demonstrations defended civil liberties and the right to assemble.

These movements did not share one programme, and they did not know my case. Their significance was cumulative. Institutions that had often spoken as if their internal operation was technical and remote were becoming subjects of public experience.

My own path was quieter and stranger. I moved through electronic forms.

A petition to the European Parliament was declared admissible in January 2025. The European Commission response described the data-protection framework and pointed enforcement back toward national authorities and courts. The private file had entered a legitimate public channel, only to be routed back toward the same national architecture.

I had not become a politician.

I had become impossible to keep entirely private.

20. The Programme Hidden Inside the Complaint

Over time, my proposals acquired a structure:

  • notify the person directly when a representative acts;
  • replace password sharing with granular authorization and acceptance;
  • make every filing, rejection and correction visible as one event chain;
  • record important outbound calls;
  • create a health-crisis pause without erasing obligations;
  • simplify tax categories around invoice data where possible;
  • let the administration prepare a proposed return rather than force every small worker to reconstruct data the administration already holds;
  • strengthen worker protection so that a nominal enterprise route is not the price of employment;
  • introduce new tax systems in parallel, test them, then retire the old path;
  • use AI to categorize and explain, not to hide responsibility behind another opaque decision.

The important change was personal. I had moved from demanding that somebody repair my account to asking how the next person could avoid entering the account in the first place.

That is political in the broad sense, but it did not begin with a party.

21. Four Years Later

In spring 2026, Hungary changed government.

The election gave the new Tisza-led majority enough seats to alter institutions that had appeared fixed. The new government described its programme through rule of law, judicial independence, anti-corruption and restored public trust. Critics warned that rapid constitutional change could reproduce the same procedural weakness it claimed to repair.

Both statements matter.

A system cannot restore trust merely by changing who controls the speed.

One sentence from my 2022 messages now acquired an uncanny echo. It had combined an enormous demand, a period of twenty years and violent language about the rule of law. In 2022 it looked detached from ordinary political possibility. Four years later, public actors were openly describing a change of regime and a restoration of the rule of law.

It was not prophecy. It was irony powerful enough to make time feel badly edited.

22. Two Letters to Venice

The constitutional conflict eventually reached the Venice Commission.

Tamás Sulyok, then President of the Republic, asked the Commission to assess the attempt to end his mandate. His questions were dated 29 May and supplemented on 4 June 2026. He argued from the position of the highest office at risk.

On 5 June, I sent my own message to the same institution.

I wrote from the opposite end of the state. My submission argued that debates about Sulyok, rule of law and human dignity should be read beside the way an ordinary citizen could experience tax administration, police procedure, forensic interpretation, clemency and years of uncertainty.

The two submissions were not equal in authority, quality or legal purpose.

That is precisely why the crossing matters.

The President defended the constitutional security of his office. A defendant asked the Commission to look at the constitutional insecurity of a person below the offices.

In July, a Venice Commission delegation met the President, the Prime Minister, ministers and the parliamentary Speaker. Public reporting showed consultation and caution rather than a final opinion that resolved every issue before Parliament acted.

The same institution had received warnings from the top and the bottom while Hungary's constitutional order was visibly between states.

23. When Seven Judges Step Aside

Venice was not Sulyok's only route.

On 11 June, he turned to the Constitutional Court for an interpretation of the limits around constitutional amendment and removal. The Court had fifteen members. Seven declared that they were personally and directly affected and excluded themselves from the matter.

The full sitting needed ten.

With only eight available, the Court could not form the quorum required to hear the matter, and it disappeared from the agenda before a substantive decision.

The Court had not literally lost half its membership. Nearly half had stepped out of one case. The visual meaning was nevertheless extraordinary: the body asked to resolve a constitutional conflict divided over whether it could even sit inside the conflict.

This occurred while my own writings were trying to reach constitutional review from below.

At one scale stood a President, an urgent request and a Court unable to assemble itself around the question. At the other stood one citizen, a laptop and an AI assistant trying to translate lived chaos into an admissible legal route.

Their authority was radically different. Their shared image was the distance between having a constitutional question and obtaining a constitutional answer.

My own route had already met that distance. The Constitutional Court received my complaint through the trial court, then stopped before the factual substance because the criminal case had not yet produced a first-instance, let alone a final, decision. The President's case was blocked because too many judges stepped aside. Mine, as I experienced it, was stopped because I had arrived at the constitutional door before ordinary procedure had finished with me.

Different cases had reached the same architectural fact: having a constitutional question does not guarantee a room in which anyone will answer it.

24. The List of Offices

After the election, the new Prime Minister publicly called for the departure of officials appointed to long terms across the old system. Reporting named the President, Prosecutor General, heads of the Constitutional Court, Curia and National Office for the Judiciary, State Audit Office, Competition Authority and Media Authority.

The list was dramatic because it described how power can survive an election. A government may leave while office-holders, boards, rules, foundations and institutional habits remain.

It was also dangerous for the opposite reason. If replacing a government means that every inconvenient office-holder can be removed through the same speed and constitutional creativity once criticized in the old system, personnel change can arrive before rule-of-law repair.

Events did not follow one identical route. The public-media structure and its leaders changed. Sulyok's mandate ended. New age and term rules meant that four of the fifteen constitutional judges then sitting—including the Court's President—were due to leave on 1 September. Other offices faced different legal procedures, political pressure or unfinished negotiations.

The correct image is not a row of heads falling in one cut.

It is a wall of institutional portraits, each moving on a different hinge while one person below them is still trying to learn what will happen at his next hearing.

25. The Empty Presidential Chair

On 18 July 2026, Sulyok signed the constitutional amendment that ended his own mandate.

The parliamentary Speaker became interim President. At the time of this draft, a new President had not yet been elected.

The empty chair was not a verdict in my case. It belonged to a country that had decided continuity was no longer enough.

Whether the replacement deserves trust depends on how it treats the same problems when speed, power and inconvenience become its own.

Part Seven — The System We Build Instead

26. The Product Returns

For years, MyScoutee had asked how people could be filtered without being reduced to a verdict.

The legal story returned the question in a harsher form.

What should a system preserve before it classifies a person?

Direct notice. Visible actions. Consent that can be withdrawn. A record of who did what. A route to correction. Private context rather than public humiliation. Reciprocal evidence rather than one unanswerable score. Enough human space for the next meeting to change the meaning of the previous one.

MyScoutee cannot repair a tax authority, court or constitution. A social product also has its own capacity for harm. Ratings can become gossip. Automation can become coercion. Matching can hide a judgment inside a number. Local operators can become unaccountable if the shared core provides no meaningful exit.

The lesson of Part II is therefore not that my product already contains the answer.

It is that the product must survive the question.

27. Humour Is a Human Audit Trail

There is one quality no event log can fully capture.

In rooms where my future was being discussed, I sometimes made people smile. The police uniform remained. The judge remained the judge. I remained the defendant. Nothing procedural changed.

Yet the smile recorded that the roles were not the whole people.

Humour was not disrespect for the seriousness of the case. It was an informal audit trail of humanity: proof only that, for one second, several people could see the absurdity together.

The word was not added years later to make the story more literary. In one 2024 submission, I wrote that the frightening part was in the absurdity. In another, I wrote that if everything had worked lawfully, I believed nothing would have happened.

The humour also appeared in writing. In one police submission, I ended by declaring the institution fired. Elsewhere, I sent institutions away to dispense justice in a pasture. A programmer with no power to dismiss the state was dismissing the state in prose.

Neither line described a real transfer of authority. Their point was the impossibility. When every office could redirect me but I could redirect none of them, sarcasm briefly reversed the arrows.

Normal conditions might have prevented the error chain. A measured transition, clear authority, direct notice, one coherent record and a body given time to recover could have left no criminal story to tell.

Instead, the system assembled a tragedy with comic timing.

28. The Invitation Changes

Part I ended by asking people to test MyScoutee in real communities.

Part II ends with a harder invitation.

Test the systems between us before pressure tests them for us.

Do not wait for the frightened taxpayer, isolated worker, exhausted accountant, overloaded official, defendant or judge to reveal every missing connection at the worst possible moment.

Design the notification. Show the delegated act. Preserve the correction. Keep the human being larger than the score. Let people leave a network without leaving their dignity inside it.

I began this period as a programmer trying to remain legal and finish a foreign contract.

I ended it—if this can yet be called an ending—sending institutional designs to a government I had not helped elect as an activist, during a constitutional transition I could not have planned.

Between those two moments, the proceeding moved from words on a screen to the material remains of Part I: the apartment my parents had helped provide, the belongings inside it, and savings built principally through work abroad. I had returned because Budapest costs made the independence earned in London usable. Now I felt that the price of trying foreign remote work from home might reach back and consume the independence that had made the attempt possible.

The next hearing was scheduled for 16 September 2026. A short reply had arrived from the new justice administration. The country had an interim President. The final legal result did not exist.

The line remains open.

MyScoutee. Test the system between us.

Notes on Evidence, Context, and the Open Ending

How to use these notes

The story above is written as memoir. These notes provide the slower second track: provenance, legal orientation, attribution limits and links that a lawyer, journalist or specialist reader can follow without forcing every scene to carry its own footnote.

Private people remain anonymous. Recollected speech is not presented as a verbatim quotation unless a recording or issued document supports it. A smile, silence or change of expression records the Founder's perception of a room; it does not establish agreement, bias or a legal conclusion. The two forensic experts are separate people. No final confiscation, financial penalty or final criminal judgment is asserted. Political change supplies public context; it does not decide the pending case or clinically resolve a contested expert opinion.

The legal links below are orientation points, not a substitute for advice. A lawyer should match every proposed argument to the law in force on the relevant date, the exact charge, the filed submissions and the complete procedural record.

The primary record

The review draft was reconstructed from the private source package described in research/SOURCE_INVENTORY.md: tax and portal evidence, authored submissions, the charge, a forensic report, correspondence, product screenshots and thirteen private recordings awaiting local transcription.

The public-interest material contains two related but distinct source lines. The first is the constructive system proposal of 1 December 2022 described in Chapter 7. It begins the design line: direct notice, visible delegated action, granular authority, an auditable correction chain, health-crisis handling and safer tax transitions.

The second is a five-page authored document dated 30 October 2025 and titled Public-Interest Action. Its cover deliberately reverses the ordinary positions: the Hungarian State is placed in the position of the accused and the Founder in the position representing the accusation. It organizes the argument under five headings: constitutional injury, data-protection injury, public-portal failures, criminal procedure and moral redress. Its final proposal imagines a KATA film fund whose cultural proceeds would support ecological restoration.

The reviewed root PDF is marked version 8; a separately signed copy is marked version 5. Their wording differs in places. Both are authored advocacy. The title alone does not establish that a court accepted the document under that procedural classification or decided its merits. The later European petition and the wider GDPR/taxation petition are separate source families again.

The raw package is not published with the book because it contains identifiers, private third-party data, medical-adjacent material and unresolved allegations.

The reviewed submissions document questions about income and financial position, refer to the apartment and record the Founder's reliance on London savings and Hungarian government-bond returns. The more specific recollection that the court asked about the apartment and belongings, and the present description of the government-bond account becoming a subject of discussion, remain memoir-layer statements unless and until the relevant hearing record is added. This edition does not claim that confiscation or a final financial penalty has been ordered.

The defence speech identifies sections 25, 26 and 27 of the Act on the Constitutional Court as possible routes. A two-page Constitutional Court letter dated 21 October 2025 records that the complaint had arrived through the trial court on 18 October while the criminal case was still pending. It explains that no first-instance decision existed, treats the section 27 route as premature, and says a complaint may be filed after a final decision if the other statutory conditions are met. It separately explains why the attempted exceptional direct route under section 26(2), including its timing requirements, was not available on the filing as presented. The letter does not examine the factual merits.

The first assigned judge's reported illness and departure remain memoir-layer until an official personnel record is isolated. The April 2026 exclusion filing documents that the motion concerned the next assigned judge. The Founder's account says a separate judge rejected that motion as unfounded and referred to the possibility of a procedural fine. The standard filing form independently contains a general statutory warning about plainly unfounded exclusion motions; it is not treated as the separate ruling. That ruling still requires isolation before any verbatim quotation.

The post-operative-leg image and the vulgar physical-comedy description are supported by authored defence material. The pasture image is presently a memoir-layer recollection and is paraphrased rather than presented as a verified quotation.

Legal reference map

The tax transition and the low-trust triangle

  • Act CXLVII of 2012 on the former KATA and small-business tax regime
  • Act XIII of 2022 on the new itemized tax for small taxpayers
  • Official explanatory memorandum to Act XIII of 2022
  • Constitutional Court Decision 29/2022 (XII. 6.) on challenges to the KATA change
  • Act CL of 2017 on the Rules of Taxation
  • Act CLI of 2017 on Tax Administration Procedure

These texts frame the tax status, transition, taxpayer responsibility, representation, communication and administrative principles around which the documentary dispute developed. The exact notice path and filing history still have to be reconstructed from the account-specific record; the statutes alone do not answer who saw which message when.

Procedure, defence and expert evidence

  • Act C of 2012, the Hungarian Criminal Code
  • Act XC of 2017 on Criminal Procedure
  • Act XXIX of 2016 on Forensic Experts
  • Act CLI of 2011 on the Constitutional Court, including the routes discussed in sections 25–27
  • The Fundamental Law of Hungary, especially the rule-of-law, privacy, fair-administration, fair-trial and remedy provisions that appear in the submissions

The exact offence, statutory range, defence route and requested remedy must be read from the charge and filed papers. This book does not infer them from the headline name of an offence.

Data, identity and European guarantees

  • Regulation (EU) 2016/679, the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), particularly the principles of processing, transparency, access, security and remedies
  • Act CXII of 2011 on Informational Self-Determination and Freedom of Information
  • Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, including dignity, private life, personal data, good administration, an effective remedy and fair-trial guarantees, subject to the Charter's scope
  • European Convention on Human Rights, particularly Articles 6 and 8
  • European Commission 2025 Rule of Law Report and country material

These instruments explain why identity-sharing, delegated action, accessible records, personal data, home, reputation, defence and effective remedies can become more than software-design questions. They do not by themselves prove a breach in this case.

Clemency social inquiry

Hungarian procedural rules identify the person preparing a social inquiry for an ordinary procedural-clemency request as a probation officer. The inquiry may describe personal, family, health, housing, employment, income and property circumstances. It is evidence assembled for the clemency file; the probation officer does not decide the request or sentence.

Official sources:

  • National Legislation Database, explanatory material for Decree 12/2022: https://njt.hu/jogszabaly/2022-12-K3-06
  • National Legislation Database, probation-service rules: https://njt.hu/jogszabaly/2013-8-20-2T

The absence of prior notice is recorded in the Founder's clemency submission. The condition of the flat, the visitor's reactions and the remembered reference to a proposed suspended sentence remain attributed memoir unless the completed social inquiry is isolated from the private archive.

Long-term work exclusion

Eurostat defines long-term unemployment at twelve months and very long-term unemployment at twenty-four months. Its definition also distinguishes active unemployment from being outside the labour force. The Founder's approximate “nine of eleven years” therefore remains memoir language for time outside conventional employment, not a claim of nine continuous years in Eurostat's unemployment category. Longitudinal research is used only as population-level context for scarring, health and re-employment; it is not used to diagnose the Founder.

This review draft does not invent the ending. Part III will own:
